title: The Inclusion Illusion
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a learning specialist for inclusion in Victorian schools, argues that explicit instruction, not inquiry, project-based learning or Universal Design for Learning, is what makes classrooms genuinely inclusive. Modelled loosely on Instructional Illusions by Kirschner, Hendrick and Heal, the post names three popular approaches that look inclusive but disadvantage novices and students with additional needs. He explains that novices lack the base knowledge to ask good questions, that open-ended projects add cognitive load, and that UDL drifts toward catering to preferences rather than functional needs. The positive half of the piece sets out an explicit inclusive lesson: entry routines, rows rather than table groups, a retrieval Do Now, accessible resources, chunked new learning with checks for understanding, and an exit reflection. His conclusion is that good explicit teaching already is inclusive teaching, because it manages extraneous load and meets students at their point of need.
points: Inquiry and project-based learning are presented as poor starting points for students with additional needs because novices lack the knowledge to frame questions and can encode misconceptions.

The author's critique of UDL is that it slides from addressing functional needs to indulging learning preferences, and that its cited meta-analyses mostly measure engagement or enjoyment rather than learning.
Seating in rows rather than table groups is defended with a cited finding that on-task behavior rose from 35% to 70% for students with special educational needs.
A concrete lesson structure is given, from entry routine and Do Now through chunked teaching with checks for understanding, with 80% and 50% class-understanding thresholds as decision rules.
The argument is that equity lives in instruction: consistent explicit teaching is itself the inclusive environment.
quotes: Too often have I seen teachers who when presented with a student with additional needs who needs a individualised learning plan ends up being provided with inquiry project after inquiry project. Sometimes relevant to the class they’re in, sometimes about areas of interest. Inquiry is fraught with issues when it comes to inclusion.

Students without the required base knowledge required for the project are unable to effectively investigate their problem and therefore can waste countless hours of learning time attempting to discover answers to their questions or potentially worse learning a misconception which is incredibly difficult to correct in future. Also, students coming from low literacy backgrounds based on their additional needs or diagnosis may struggle to find the right words they need to seek answers to their questions or may not be able to decode and understand the complex resources they find.
It sounds moral. It sounds easy to implement. But in my opinion it leads to a lethal mutation of true inclusion more often than not.

The research around the effectiveness of UDL is very interesting, despite there being numerous positive meta-analyses about its impact, when you delve deeper into the results of these students, they almost always refer to student surveys of engagement or enjoyment of class rather than student learning growth. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy if you give students exactly what the will prefer that they will enjoy class more, but this is supposed to be design for learning… are they learning more?

Having a consistent entry routine is incredibly important to set the scene for a productive class. An ideal entry routine would involve students entering the classroom quietly, taking a seat and beginning work on a task related to their prior learning.

New learning should be presented in small manageable chunks to optimize the limits of working memory/student cognitive load. This is said to be around 3 to 5 items at a time and the number reduces as the complexity of each item increases. After each new concept as been introduced the teacher should check for full class understanding before moving on. These checks for understanding (CFUs) should be presented in a variety of forms and increase in difficulty and reduce in scaffolding as the lesson progresses.

Yes, every human being is different, but how we think and learn is relatively the same based on the neuroscience of learning. Explicit teaching is vital for being inclusive in schools as it provides an environment which actively manages extraneous load and meets students at their point of need and provides scaffolds to push them further.
